title: Semantic Justifications for Multiple Interpretations of Visual Emotion Perception with Open Vocabulary
tagline: Not just which emotion, but what's in the image and why it feels that way, for any emotion you ask about.
description: PeqEMO is a family of compact vision-language models that predict an image's emotion and justify it through a Perception → Trigger → Label process, with open-vocabulary and conditioned interpretations.
tldr: PeqEMO doesn't just label an image's emotion. It explains what it sees and why that feels a certain way, and it can argue for several different emotions for the same image, each grounded in the picture.

teaser.caption: PeqEMO reads an image the way a person might: what it sees, why that feels a certain way, and which emotion follows.
teaser.todo: 10–15 s loop: an image appears, then the Perception, Trigger and Label paragraphs type out one after another.

problem.caption: The same photo can support several emotional readings.
problem.todo: One photo surrounded by 3–4 plausible emotion tags (e.g. awe, fear, excitement), each with the visual cue that supports it.

framework.caption: PeqEMO framework: a vision encoder and projector feed Qwen3-VL (LoRA-tuned), which returns a label plus a structured justification.

howitworks.caption: Perception → Trigger → Label, step by step.
howitworks.todo: Animation: highlight the image regions mentioned in Perception, then draw arrows from those cues to the Trigger sentences, then reveal the Label.

dataset.caption: Building VIA-EmoSET: EmoSet images are annotated by GLM-4.6V with Perception, Trigger and Label.
dataset.todo: Figure 2 of the paper (VIA-EmoSET construction pipeline).

emoloss.caption: Label dilution: the answer is a tiny fraction of the tokens. Emo-Loss turns its weight up.
emoloss.todo: Animation: a long justification with the 1–3 label tokens highlighted; a bar showing the label’s share of the training signal grows from ~1–2% to ~50% as λ goes from 1 to 30.

sections.title: Why emotion is hard for machines

blocks.html: Look at a photo of an abandoned room with light pouring through the door. Is it eerie? Hopeful? Sad? People disagree, and they can all explain why. Emotion in images is subjective: the same scene supports several readings, depending on what you notice.

Most emotion-recognition models ignore this. They pick one label from a fixed list and give no reason. Newer multimodal chatbots can explain themselves, but their explanations are often loosely tied to what is actually in the picture, and they still assume a single right answer.

deeper.summary: Go deeper: where existing approaches fall short

blocks.html: Visual Sentiment Analysis (VSA) has classically been image classification over a closed set of categories. Language-supervised methods and emotion-tuned multimodal LLMs (e.g. EmoVIT, Emotion-LLaMA) moved the field from predicting what emotion is present toward explaining why, but they tend to (1) treat interpretation as a single fixed prediction, (2) produce weakly grounded explanations, (3) stay tied to one taxonomy, or (4) focus on faces and people rather than general scenes.

sections.title: How it works: Perception → Trigger → Label

blocks.html: PeqEMO answers in three steps, the way a careful person would explain a feeling:

items.title: Perception
items.text: Describe only what is visible: setting, lighting, colours, the main subject.

items.title: Trigger
items.text: Explain how those visual cues could make someone feel something, as simple cause-and-effect chains.

items.title: Label
items.text: Name the emotion that follows from the evidence.

blocks.html: Because the list of allowed emotions is written into the prompt, the same model works with any emotion vocabulary, from 2 categories up to more than 25, without retraining. And because the label can be supplied instead of predicted, you can ask it: “explain why this image could feel like fear”.

deeper.summary: Go deeper: model, training and inference

items: Backbone: Qwen3-VL at 2B, 4B and 8B parameters, fine-tuned with LoRA (rank 32, α = 64, dropout 0.05) on all attention and MLP projections of both the vision encoder and the language decoder.
Cheap to train: AdamW, learning rate 5×10−5, cosine schedule, 2 epochs, with Unsloth dynamic 4-bit quantization. Every model size trains in about 30 minutes on a single RTX 3090 (24 GB).
Taxonomy-agnostic prompting: the prompt ends with Choose the final label from the allowed taxonomy: {taxonomy}, so the label space is swapped at inference time.

Two-stage inference: first the label is predicted deterministically (temperature 0, ≤15 tokens); then the response is prefilled with that label and the justification is sampled (temperature 0.75, top-p 0.8, ≤224 tokens).
Conditioned justification: prefill Predicted Label: y with any emotion y and the model writes a justification for that reading, while keeping the image and taxonomy fixed.

blocks.label: Instruction prompt
blocks.text:
You are an expert annotator for visual emotion recognition.
Analyze the image and produce a structured reasoning chain following this exact format:

Predicted Label:
[EMOTION_LABEL]
Justification:
[Detailed visual description]
[Psychological causal chains]

Choose the final label from the allowed taxonomy: {taxonomy}

blocks.html: This is the part we find most interesting. Pick an image, then pick an emotion: PeqEMO writes a justification for that emotion, pointing only at things that are really in the picture. The dataset label marks the emotion the dataset's annotators chose.

deeper.summary: Go deeper: what the model is doing here

blocks.html: These are conditioned justifications (paper §5.5, Appendix F). The image and the 8-class EmoSet taxonomy stay fixed; only the prefilled label changes. The Perception paragraph stays faithful to the image, while the Trigger paragraph selects different visual cues to build each reading. The dense pansies read as playful under amusement, but as overwhelming clutter under fear. Some texts end in “…” where the paper's figure truncates them.

sections.title: VIA-EmoSET: teaching the model to explain

blocks.html: To learn this kind of answer, PeqEMO needs examples of it. We built VIA-EmoSET: 94,481 images from EmoSet, each paired with a Perception / Trigger / Label explanation written by an open vision-language model (GLM-4.6V). There is no proprietary annotation pipeline, so anyone can reproduce it.

deeper.summary: Go deeper: why EmoSet, and the annotation rules

items: EmoSet has 118,102 human-verified images over 8 balanced emotions (amusement, anger, awe, contentment, disgust, excitement, fear, sadness): the largest human-annotated visual emotion dataset, about 5× larger than FI. Larger web datasets such as WEBEmo (~268k) derive labels from noisy metadata.
Perception: 2–4 sentences describing only observable details (background, lighting, colours, subject). No emotions, intentions or story.
Trigger: 3–5 sentences of causal chains, visual element → psychological mechanism → emotional implication, written in plain language and referencing only the Perception.
Label: the EmoSet ground truth. The annotator is told the correct label and must genuinely support it from the image. Responses are capped at 512 tokens.

sections.title: Emo-Loss: don't let the answer get drowned out

blocks.html: A justification is a few hundred words long; the emotion label is one to three. With ordinary training, every word counts the same, so the label contributes only about 1–2% of the learning signal. The model gets very good at writing fluent explanations and less careful about the actual answer. We call this label dilution.
The fix is simple: during training, the label tokens count 30× more. That roughly balances “get the emotion right” against “explain it well”.

Visual emotion perception is framed as conditional sequence generation: given image I and a prompt with taxonomy T, the model outputs a sequence containing a label ŷ ∈ T and a justification J. Emo-Loss is token-weighted cross-entropy: tokens belonging to the label get weight λ = 30, all others weight 1. The value is a balancing heuristic, chosen to roughly equalize the cumulative contribution of the 1–3 label tokens with the full justification. It reduces fluent but label-inconsistent outputs.

Small, cheap models, but strong ones. Even the 2B version beats the emotion-specialized EmoVIT-8B on average, the 4B and 8B versions beat GPT-5.2 on a mixed benchmark, and independent AI judges prefer PeqEMO's explanations.

blocks.html: Caveat: LLM judges have known verbosity, position and self-preference biases. We use three judges from different model families and randomize A/B order, but judge–expert agreement in specialized domains is around 60–68%, so treat these scores as a complementary signal to the accuracy benchmarks.

sections.title: What it gets right, and where it disagrees

blocks.html: When PeqEMO is right, its explanation points at the exact cues a person would. When it “fails”, the explanation often shows a different but reasonable reading, which says as much about single-label benchmarks as about the model.

items.text: The bright sunlight and clear skies create a sense of warmth and openness, which can evoke feelings of comfort and relaxation. The casual attire of the subjects, light clothing suitable for warm weather, and their relaxed posture while walking hand-in-hand suggest ease and familiarity, fostering a connection between them that implies satisfaction. The presence of tropical vegetation and resort-style architecture reinforces an association with vacations or pleasant getaways, contributing to an implication of peaceful enjoyment.

The open mouths of both dogs displaying visible teeth create an immediate sense of threat, as bared canines are a common signal of aggression in animals. This visual cue triggers an instinctive psychological mechanism that prepares viewers for potential danger or conflict, leading to heightened alertness. The close physical proximity between the two dogs further emphasizes their confrontational stance, reinforcing the implication of tension and hostility in the interaction.

items.note: Perspective: the dinosaur expresses anger, but the viewer feels fear.
items.text: The dinosaur's wide-open mouth with sharp teeth, a common visual cue for danger, triggers an instinctive sense of threat. The combination of the dinosaur's imposing size and the artificial, enclosed setting creates a sense of being trapped, which can evoke feelings of unease. The contrast between the bright teeth and the surroundings enhances the visual impact of the threat, making the scene feel potentially frightening.

items.note: Co-occurring emotions: suspenseful play is both fun and scary.
items.text: The cool blue lighting and grid structures create a playful, futuristic atmosphere that can evoke a sense of lightheartedness. The figures' raised hands and dynamic postures suggest movement and energy, which often leads to feelings of amusement. The high contrast between the illuminated grids and the dark background adds visual interest, making the scene feel engaging and entertaining.

items.note: Cultural priors: labelled amusement because it's a theme park, but clowns are widely associated with unease.
items.text: The clown's exaggerated facial features, such as the large red nose and wide mouth, trigger a psychological mechanism of threat detection, as these distorted proportions can evoke a sense of unease. The bright, chaotic lighting and the carnival setting, which often includes unpredictable elements, create an atmosphere of uncertainty, leading to a feeling of discomfort.

items: Emotion is subjective. Outputs are plausible interpretations, not psychological ground truth. Datasets also blur the expressed emotion of a subject with the evoked emotion of the viewer.
Inherited biases. PeqEMO picks up priors from its training data, such as landscapes → awe or clowns → fear, which may not match every culture or person.

Intended use: affective-computing research and creative work (advertising, design, film). Not for surveillance, mass emotion monitoring, or high-stakes decisions such as hiring, law enforcement or mental-health triage. Any use involving real people needs consent and human review.
